title: An Inspector Calls: context and the essay question
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: modern drama, An Inspector Calls
AO3: contexts; the 30-mark essay and AO4

tips.title: Two dates, one line
tips.body: Set in 1912, written and first performed in 1945, London in October 1946. Every forecast in Act 1 and the warning in Act 3 are heard across those thirty-three years. That is the first sentence of context in almost any essay on this play.

tips.title: One fact, one choice, one sentence
tips.body: The war explains the warning; the broadcasts explain the plainness; the party explains the politics; the missing welfare state explains the chain. Never write a fact without the choice it explains.

tips.title: Bolted-on context
tips.body: If a sentence could be deleted without losing anything about the play, it is history, not context. The examiners describe that as awareness of contextual factors, and it sits in the middle of the ladder at best.

tips.title: The bullets are the plan
tips.body: Every question has two bullets: what the character says and does, and how Priestley presents them. AO1 across the whole play, then AO2. Turn them into a plan in two minutes and the essay has its shape.

tips.title: Forty-five minutes, then stop
tips.body: Thirty-four marks of ninety-six is a third of the paper. Overrunning on the essay is paid for at the end in the unseen poetry, which is thirty-two marks and cannot be rushed.

tips.title: The ladder's words
tips.body: Narrative at Level 1; supported at 2; explained at 3; clear at 4; thoughtful and developed at 5; convincing, critical and conceptualised at 6. Know which word your paragraph is earning.

why.matters: A play is written at one moment about another, for an audience living in a third, and the meaning lives in the gaps. Priestley set his in 1912, wrote it in 1945 and knew his audience had just voted on the very question it asks. The exam gives six of every thirty marks to context, and its own words are exact: the top level explores contextual factors, the middle merely shows awareness of them. The difference is whether a fact explains a choice. Knowing 1912, 1945 and Priestley's life is the easy part; knowing which choice each fact explains is what the marks are for, and it is also how the essay itself is planned and timed.

examples.title: Reading the date on anything
examples.body: A newspaper column, a speech, a song: each was written on a date, for people living through something, and it reads differently once the date is known. A wartime broadcast, a manifesto from an election year, a poem written the week a war ended: the date is not background, it is part of what the words mean. Priestley's two dates are a training case for reading everything else that way.

examples.title: The forty-five-minute essay
examples.body: Every timed essay, in an exam or an interview task, is the same problem: a question to take apart, a plan to make in minutes, and a clock. The habit of turning the question's own wording into a plan, and sharing the time by the marks, is what makes a good answer possible under pressure. Literature Paper 2 is one of the first places it is practised for real.

steps.title: 1912: the world the characters live in
steps.body:
Priestley chose 1912 with care. It was the last confident year before the war, and everything Birling is sure of was about to be proved wrong.

**No welfare state.** A sacked worker had no unemployment pay from the state that would have supported a girl like Eva Smith; the old age pension of 1908 was for the over-seventies, and national insurance, which began in 1911, covered only some workers in some trades. A girl without work had a shop, a bar or a charity. Every door in the chain is one of those.

**Strikes.** The national coal strike of spring 1912 was the largest the country had seen. Birling's speech waves away labour trouble as something that has passed; the audience knows it had barely begun.

**The Titanic.** She sailed in April 1912 and sank on her maiden voyage, within weeks of the evening of the play. Birling calls her unsinkable.

**Women.** No woman could vote in a general election in 1912, and a working woman's choices were narrow. The play's three women stand at three levels of a system none of them made.

Each of these earns a sentence in an essay only when it explains something on stage: why the chain has the links it has, why Birling's confidence is dramatic irony, why the girl had nowhere to go.

rows: No unemployment pay; charity for the poor
The girl's options after the works: a shop, a bar, a committee
Birling's dismissal of labour trouble; the strike at his works
The Titanic sails in April and sinks
No vote for women in a general election; narrow work for working women
Eva's life; Sheila kept from unpleasantness; Mrs Birling's committee

steps.title: 1945: the audience's world
steps.body:
The play was written in 1945, in the months around the end of the Second World War, and first performed in Moscow and Leningrad that year because no London theatre was free. It opened in London in October 1946.

**What the audience had lived through.** Two wars since 1912. The first, which Birling says will never come, began two years after the evening of the play; the second had just ended. The Inspector's warning about fire and blood and anguish was, to them, a description of their own lives.

**What the audience had just chosen.** The general election of July 1945 returned a Labour government committed to the welfare state proposed in the Beveridge Report of 1942: a health service, insurance against unemployment, help for exactly the people the Birlings turned away. The play's argument about one body was that year's politics, and the audience had just voted on it.

**How to use it.** The 1945 audience is the reason for the dramatic irony and the reason for the message. A sentence such as *Priestley set the warning in 1912 so that an audience of 1945 would hear it as history* connects the date to a method.

check.prompt: How does the July 1945 election help explain a choice Priestley made in the play?
check.solution: The London audience of 1946 watched a committee refuse a pregnant girl a year after voting for a welfare state that would not. Priestley stages the world they had rejected. That sentence turns an election result into an explanation of a scene, which is how context earns marks.

steps.title: Priestley: the life behind the choices
steps.body:
Priestley was born in Bradford, 13 September 1894. He volunteered in September 1914, served with the Duke of Wellington's Regiment, was buried alive by a trench mortar in June 1916 and was later gassed. His BBC radio Postscripts on Sunday nights in 1940 reached audiences of up to sixteen million and were taken off the air after complaints about their politics. He co-founded the Common Wealth Party in 1942, and was later a founding member of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament in 1958. He died on 14 August 1984.

**Each fact explains a choice.** The war is why the warning about fire and blood is spoken by a man who means it. The broadcasts are why the Inspector talks past the family to the audience with a broadcaster's plainness. The party is why the speech about one body is politics, not sentiment. Bradford is why the town is an industrial one and the family a manufacturer's.

**What not to do.** A paragraph of biography with no play in it earns almost nothing. One fact, one choice, one sentence, is the shape that scores.

rows: An industrial town; a manufacturer's family
Buried alive by a trench mortar, 1916
The warning about fire and blood, spoken by a survivor
The Inspector's plainness; speaking past the family
One body as politics, not sentiment

The run of dates from Bradford to 1942 is a list, the sentence calling the play a socialist play is a label, and the sentence about the broadcasts being popular is a claim about popularity. Context is a reason for a method, not a substitute for one.

steps.title: The forms Priestley borrowed
steps.body:
A play's form is a context too, and this one borrows three.

**The morality play.** Medieval drama in which a figure of Everyman is visited by figures of Death or Conscience and made to account for his life. The Inspector calls on a family and makes each account for one act. The name Eva, close to Eve, and the surname Smith, the commonest there is, make the girl an Everywoman.

**The whodunnit.** A detective, a death, a house full of suspects questioned one at a time. Priestley takes the form and turns it over: the question is not who did it but how each of them helped, and the detective may not exist.

**The well-made play.** The nineteenth-century form of tight plotting, a single setting, continuous time and a curtain line at the end of each act. Priestley keeps all of it, which is why the play feels like a machine closing.

A sentence naming the form and what Priestley does with it is AO3 and AO2 together: a context, and a method.

check.prompt: What does Priestley change when he borrows the shape of a whodunnit?
check.solution: The form is kept and its point reversed. A whodunnit ends by isolating one guilty person; this play ends by refusing to, and by leaving the audience unsure whether the detective existed. Naming the form and the reversal is context used as method.

steps.title: The mark scheme's ladder, and the four marks for AO4
steps.body:
The thirty marks are given in six levels, and the words that name them are worth knowing, because they describe what the examiner is looking for at each step.

**Level 6, 26 to 30:** convincing, critical analysis and exploration; a conceptualised approach to the whole task; judicious references; fine-grained analysis of methods. **Level 5, 21 to 25:** thoughtful, developed consideration. **Level 4, 16 to 20:** clear understanding; a clear, explained response with effective references. **Level 3, 11 to 15:** explained, structured comments. **Level 2, 6 to 10:** supported, relevant comments. **Level 1, 1 to 5:** simple, explicit comments, narrative or descriptive in approach.

Twelve marks are for AO1, twelve for AO2 and six for AO3 within those thirty, so an essay with no methods cannot pass the middle of the ladder however well it knows the play.

**AO4, four marks, on this question only in Paper 2.** High performance, 4: consistent accuracy and effective control of meaning. Intermediate, 2 to 3: considerable accuracy and range. Threshold, 1: reasonable accuracy, errors not hindering meaning. Five minutes of checking is usually worth two of these marks.

visuals.alt: A table of the six levels of the mark scheme for the thirty-mark essay, with the marks for each and the words the examiners use

check.prompt: The word the Level 6 descriptor uses for the approach it wants is conceptualised. What does that mean in practice?
check.solution: Conceptualised means led by a concept: an idea about what the writer built, which the paragraphs then demonstrate. The scheme sets it against a response that is narrative or descriptive in approach, and it is the single biggest difference between the top of the ladder and the middle.

markScheme.description: The essay has an idea about the whole text and every paragraph serves it, rather than working through points one by one

options: The essay uses as many technical terms as possible, so that the examiner can see that the student knows the vocabulary of literary analysis
The essay covers every scene in the play in order, so that nothing in the text is left out of the answer
The essay is longer than the others, because more ideas need more words to explain them fully
The essay has an idea about the whole text and every paragraph serves it, rather than working through points one by one

steps.title: Turn a fact into an explanation
steps.body:
Take each fact and write the sentence that turns it into an explanation of something Priestley did. The test is simple: does the sentence mention a choice in the play?

1. The Titanic sank in April 1912.
2. There was no state help for an unemployed girl in 1912.
3. Priestley's broadcasts in 1940 reached sixteen million people.
4. The play was first performed in 1945, the year of the election.

Then do the reverse: take one choice, the delayed doubt about the Inspector, and find the context that explains it.

check.solution: The sentence about building the chain out of the only doors open to a sacked girl names a choice and says the history is why it has the shape it has. The sentence calling the lack of help unfair states the fact, the one about 1912 and 1945 compares the dates, and the one about the charity turning her away retells what happened to the girl. Only the sentence about the chain explains something Priestley did.

steps.title: Context that explains a choice
steps.body:
The top of the ladder asks for convincing exploration of contextual factors, and the middle warns against context bolted on. The difference is whether the sentence has a choice in it.

**Three sentences that score.** *Priestley set the play in 1912 so that an audience of 1945 would hear Birling's forecasts as dramatic irony.* *He gives the committee to Mrs Birling because in 1912 the charity of ladies was what stood where a welfare state would.* *He wrote the Inspector's speech in the year of the election that would build that state, and the speech is its argument.*

**One that does not.** *In 1912 there was a strict class system and no welfare state, and women could not vote.* True, and useless, because nothing in the play is explained.

**Alternative readings are context too.** The play as a morality play, as a whodunnit reversed, as a ghost story, as a political argument: naming two readings in a sentence and saying what each explains is the exploration of interpretations the top descriptor names.

boxes.body: A method, a line, a scene: something Priestley did

check.prompt: Which of these would the examiners place in the middle of the ladder rather than the top, and why?
check.solution: The paragraph of class system, strikes and women followed by a separate paragraph on the play is context bolted on: accurate history with no choice in it, which the scheme describes as awareness of contextual factors rather than exploration of them. The sentences about the committee, the whodunnit and the election are exactly what scores, and none is disqualified by being short, about genre or about politics.

steps.title: Context, question, marks
steps.body:
Three things to carry into the paper, apart from the play itself.

- **1912:** no welfare state, so the chain is the doors a girl could try; the coal strike; the Titanic in April; no vote for women in a general election.
- **1945:** two wars since 1912; the July election and the welfare state; first performed in Moscow and Leningrad, then London in October 1946; the audience heard the warning as history.
- **Priestley:** Bradford 1894; buried alive in 1916; Postscripts to sixteen million in 1940; the Common Wealth Party in 1942. One fact, one choice, one sentence.
- **Forms:** morality play, whodunnit reversed, well-made play; naming one and what Priestley does with it is context and method together.
- **The essay:** about 45 minutes; the bullets are the shape; plan from the character's moments; the ladder runs from narrative at Level 1 to conceptualised at Level 6; five minutes checking for the four AO4 marks.

Context that explains a choice scores. Context that fills a paragraph does not.

questions.prompt: Write the opening paragraph of an answer to the June 2024 question on how Priestley uses the Inspector to suggest the need for social change. The paragraph should state a conceptualised idea, name a method, use one checked quotation, and include one sentence of context that explains a choice.
questions.solution: Priestley builds the Inspector as the instrument by which a family, and an audience, is made to see that a society is one body, and every method he gives him serves that end. The questioning is forensic, one person at a time in the order they met the girl, so that shared responsibility is demonstrated link by link before it is ever stated; the plainness of the Inspector's statements, set against the family's evasions, makes the case for change without a speech, until the speech comes and lands as a verdict: “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other”. Priestley wrote the play in 1945, in the year of an election that would build the welfare state for exactly the people the Birlings turned away, and he set it in 1912 so that an audience which had just voted for that change would watch the world it had rejected refuse the lesson, one door at a time. The need for social change is not argued by the Inspector so much as shown by him: the play is the proof, and he is the method of the proof.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how the form of the play, as a morality play, a whodunnit reversed and a well-made play, serves Priestley's purpose. Treat each form as a context and say what Priestley does with it.
questions.solution: Priestley's play borrows three forms and bends each to his argument. From the medieval morality play he takes the visitor who makes a representative person account for a life: the Inspector calls on a family and the girl with the commonest name in the country, one of the “millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths”, stands for everyone, so that a drawing room becomes a judgement on a class. From the whodunnit he takes a death, a detective and a house of suspects questioned one at a time, and then reverses the point of the form: the question is not who did it but how each of them helped, “each of you helped to kill her”, and the detective is left unproved, so that the last act cannot isolate a culprit and must instead show the family choosing what to believe. From the well-made play he keeps the single room, the continuous time and the curtain line at the end of every act, which is why the evening closes on the family like a machine and why the telephone can restart it. Each form is a context the audience of 1945 knew, and each is turned so that its familiar comfort, the ending that solves everything, is refused. Priestley wanted an audience choosing what to rebuild to leave the theatre without that comfort, and the forms are how he took it away.

questions.prompt: A student opens an essay with a paragraph on Priestley's life: Bradford, the war, the broadcasts, the party. Where does the mark scheme place that paragraph, and what would fix it?
questions.solution: Biography with no play in it is awareness, not exploration. The fix is not more history but a choice: the war explains the warning, the broadcasts explain the plainness, the party explains the politics. One fact, one choice, one sentence, and it moves up the ladder.

markScheme.description: In the lower levels, as awareness of contextual factors with nothing explained; fixed by attaching each fact to one choice in the play in a single sentence

options: In the lower levels, as awareness of contextual factors with nothing explained; fixed by attaching each fact to one choice in the play in a single sentence
At the top, because it shows thorough research into the writer and his times, which is what AO3 rewards; nothing at all needs fixing, and the paragraph could be longer still
In the middle, because biography is worth some marks but not many; fixed by making it longer
Nowhere, because AO3 is not assessed on the modern text question; fixed by deleting it

questions.prompt: Why does Priestley set the play in 1912 rather than in 1945, the year he wrote it?
questions.solution: The gap between the two dates is the play's engine: dramatic irony in Act 1, and a warning heard as history in Act 3. Setting it in 1945 would have lost both. The choice of date is a method, and explaining it is the AO3 the scheme calls exploration.

markScheme.description: So that the audience knows what the characters cannot, and every forecast Birling makes, and every warning the Inspector gives, is heard against thirty-three years of history

options: Because the Titanic and the coal strike were interesting events that audiences would enjoy hearing about
So that the audience knows what the characters cannot, and every forecast Birling makes, and every warning the Inspector gives, is heard against thirty-three years of history
Because plays about the present were not allowed on the London stage in 1946 by the censor, and every new play therefore had to be set at least a generation in the past, as this one is
Because Priestley wanted to write a historical drama about the Edwardian age and its manners

examTechnique.body:
**Context explains a choice.** Six of the thirty marks. One fact, one choice, one sentence, and never a paragraph of history on its own.

**Learn the two dates and what each does.** 1912 gives the dramatic irony and the doors of the chain; 1945 gives the audience that heard the warning as its own past and had just voted for the welfare state.

**Forms are context too.** Morality play, whodunnit reversed, well-made play: naming one and what Priestley does with it is AO3 and AO2 in a sentence.

**Plan from the bullets, share the time by the marks.** About 45 minutes; five to plan, thirty-five to write, five to check for the four AO4 marks.

**Know the ladder.** Narrative at the bottom, conceptualised at the top. Every paragraph should be earning a word from Level 5 or 6.
examinerErrors: Opening with a paragraph of history or biography that explains no choice in the play.
Getting the dates wrong: 1912 and 1945 are the frame of every contextual point.
Overrunning on the essay and leaving too little time for the poetry, which carries more marks in total.
Ignoring the two bullets under the question, which are the shape the examiners expect.
Writing without checking, and losing two or three of the four AO4 marks to slips a re-read would have caught.
Treating context as a separate paragraph at the end rather than as a sentence inside each point.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer wears its context lightly and exactly: a sentence at a time, each attached to a choice Priestley made, so that 1912, 1945 and the writer's own war appear as reasons for methods rather than as background. It names the form the play borrows and what Priestley does with it, offers an alternative reading in a sentence, and reads the two dates as the source of both the dramatic irony and the message. It is planned from the question's bullets, led by an idea about the whole text, timed to forty-five minutes, and checked, so that the four marks for accuracy are taken as well as the thirty for the argument.
